title: Numbers & the Number System
weightage: 6-9 questions across the Mathematics and Maths-Pedagogy halves of CTET Paper I
intro: Numbers is where CTET Paper I begins, and it carries more weight than most candidates expect. The Mathematics section tests whether you can actually do the arithmetic - read a place value chart, write a number in expanded form, convert XIV to 14 - while the pedagogy half asks something harder: do you understand how a six-year-old builds these ideas, and why she makes the mistakes she does. The two are tied together in almost every question. A typical item shows you a child writing 'five hundred six' as 56 and asks what the child has misunderstood; you score the mark only if you can name the missing concept (zero as a placeholder) rather than just spot the wrong answer. This chapter walks through the nine ideas the exam keeps returning to - counting, number names, place value, expanded form, comparing and ordering, patterns, parity, and basic Roman numerals - and it keeps the classroom in view throughout, because that is what CTET is really examining.

formulas.title: Place value (base-10 columns and the two values of a digit)

items.name: Face value
items.formula: The digit itself, ignoring position. In 3582 the face value of 8 is 8.

items.name: Place value
items.formula: Face value x value of its place. In 3582 the place value of 8 is 8 x 10 = 80.

items.name: Add / subtract rule
items.formula: Smaller after larger adds (VI = 6); smaller before larger subtracts (IV = 4, IX = 9, XL = 40, XC = 90)

items.name: Repetition rule
items.formula: I, X, C repeat up to three times; V and L are never repeated and never subtracted

items.name: Even number
items.formula: Ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8; can be written as 2n

items.name: Odd number
items.formula: Ends in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9; can be written as 2n + 1

topics.name: Counting
topics.details: Counting looks trivial to an adult, but it rests on a handful of principles that CTET tests directly. To count a set of objects a child must recite number names in a fixed order (the stable-order principle), tag each object once and only once (one-to-one correspondence), and understand that the last number said is the total (cardinality) - and that the total does not change if you start from a different object (order irrelevance). Three kinds of counting matter for the exam. Forward counting recites numbers in increasing order from any starting point (start at 5, go three steps: 5, 6, 7, 8) and builds the idea of 'one more', the seed of addition. Backward counting goes the other way (12, 11, 10, 9) and underpins subtraction and 'one less'; children often stall crossing a decade, getting stuck going 21, 20, then hesitating. Skip counting jumps by a fixed amount - 2, 4, 6, 8 or 5, 10, 15, 20 or 10, 20, 30 - and is the bridge to multiplication tables and equal grouping. The teaching order runs concrete to abstract: real counters and number-line hops first, charts and mental counting later.

solved.problem: A child counting a row of seven beads points to two beads while saying 'four'. Which counting principle has she broken?
solved.solution: One-to-one correspondence - each object must be tagged with exactly one number word. Pointing to two beads on a single count violates it, so the total will be wrong.

solved.problem: Complete the skip-counting series: 5, 10, 15, 20, __ . What is the rule and the next term?
solved.solution: The rule is add 5 each time (skip counting by 5s). The next term is 20 + 5 = 25.

solved.problem: Counting backward from 22: 22, 21, 20, __ . A child says '10'. What likely went wrong, and what is correct?
solved.solution: The child confused the decade boundary. The correct term is 19 - after 20 comes 19, not a jump to 10. Crossing decades backward is a known sticking point.

solved.problem: Why is skip counting by 2s considered a foundation for multiplication?
solved.solution: Each jump represents one equal group of 2, so 2, 4, 6, 8 is really 1, 2, 3, 4 groups of two. That equal-grouping idea is exactly what multiplication formalises.

unsolved.problem: Forward counting from 8 by single steps gives 8, 9, __, 11. Fill the blank.
Skip counting by 10s starting at 10: 10, 20, 30, __ . Next term?
The principle that the last number you say while counting is the total number of objects is called:
Counting backward from 15 by ones: 15, 14, 13, __ . Fill the blank.

topics.name: Number Names
topics.details: A number name is the word form of a numeral - 'forty-three' for 43, 'five hundred six' for 506. Reading and writing number names is really place value spoken aloud, and CTET often disguises a place value question as a naming one. The child has to map the spoken or written words onto the right columns: 'five hundred six' means five hundreds, zero tens, six ones, so the numeral is 506, not 56. The zero in the tens place has no spoken word, which is exactly where children slip, dropping it and writing 56. Reversal is the other common error - hearing 'forty-three' and writing 34 because they record the words in the order they hear the sounds rather than by place. Good teaching links the oral name straight to the place value reading: say 'fifty-three' and immediately show 5 tens and 3 ones, so the word and the column structure are learned together rather than the name being memorised as an isolated label.

solved.problem: Write the numeral for 'five hundred six'.
solved.solution: 506. Five hundreds, zero tens, six ones. The unspoken zero must be written in the tens place to hold the column - writing 56 loses the hundreds.

solved.problem: A child writes 'forty-three' as 34. Name the error.
solved.solution: A reversal error - the child wrote the digits in the order the sounds arrived rather than by place value. Forty-three is 4 tens and 3 ones, so 43.

solved.problem: Write the number name for 270.
solved.solution: Two hundred seventy. Two hundreds, seven tens, zero ones - the zero ones contributes no spoken word.

solved.problem: Which numeral is 'one thousand two hundred thirty-four'?
solved.solution: 1234. One thousand, two hundreds, three tens, four ones, read straight down the place value columns.

unsolved.problem: Write the numeral for 'nine hundred forty'.
hints: Nine hundreds, four tens, zero ones.
Hold the ones place with a zero.
Four hundreds, zero tens, eight ones.

unsolved.problem: A pupil writes 'three hundred seven' as 37. What concept is missing?
unsolved.answer: Zero as a placeholder (in the tens place)

topics.name: Place Value
topics.details: Place value is the single most important idea in this chapter and the one CTET tests hardest. In our base-10 system the value of a digit depends on where it sits: reading right to left the columns are ones (10^0 = 1), tens (10^1 = 10), hundreds (10^2 = 100) and thousands (10^3 = 1000). Take 347: the 7 is in the ones place (7 x 1 = 7), the 4 in the tens (4 x 10 = 40), the 3 in the hundreds (3 x 100 = 300). This forces the distinction the exam loves. Face value is the digit by itself, regardless of position - in 3582 the face value of 8 is just 8. Place value is the face value multiplied by the column's worth - in 3582 the place value of 8 is 8 x 10 = 80. Zero earns its keep as a placeholder: it marks an empty column, which is the only thing separating 45, 405 and 450. The teaching arc is concrete-representational-abstract - bundles of ten straws and base-10 blocks before pictures before bare numerals - with trading games (ten ones for one ten, ten tens for one hundred) to drive home the ten-to-one structure.

solved.problem: In the number 347, state the place value of the digit 4.
solved.solution: 4 is in the tens place, so its place value is 4 x 10 = 40.

solved.problem: In 3582, give the face value and the place value of 8.
solved.solution: Face value of 8 is 8 (the digit itself). Place value is 8 x 10 = 80, since 8 sits in the tens place.

solved.problem: In 5347, what is the place value of 5?
solved.solution: 5 is in the thousands place, so its place value is 5 x 1000 = 5000.

solved.problem: What does the 0 contribute in 405, and why does it matter?
solved.solution: The 0 sits in the tens place, meaning zero tens. It is a placeholder that keeps the 4 in the hundreds column - without it the number would collapse to 45.

unsolved.problem: In 729, what is the place value of 2?
In 6184, give the face value of 1.
In 2860, what is the place value of 8?
Which digit acts as a placeholder in 304?

topics.name: Expanded Form
topics.details: Expanded form writes a number as the sum of the place values of its digits, making visible what each digit actually contributes. It is place value written out long-hand: 56 = 50 + 6, or stated fully 5 tens + 6 ones. The exam likes numbers with a zero, because that is where children stumble: 409 = 400 + 0 + 9, usually tidied to 400 + 9, where the zero tens simply add nothing. A four-digit case shows the full structure - 1234 = 1000 + 200 + 30 + 4, that is 1 thousand + 2 hundreds + 3 tens + 4 ones. The classic error is to expand by face value instead of place value, writing 321 = 3 + 2 + 1; the correction is 321 = 300 + 20 + 1, because the 3 is worth three hundreds and the 2 is worth two tens. Going the other way - collapsing 700 + 50 + 2 back to 752 - is the standard reverse task, and getting both directions fluent is what the exam checks.

solved.problem: Write 56 in expanded form.
solved.solution: 56 = 50 + 6, that is 5 tens + 6 ones.

solved.problem: Write 409 in expanded form.
solved.solution: 409 = 400 + 0 + 9 = 400 + 9. The zero in the tens place contributes nothing, but it still holds the column.

solved.problem: Write 1234 in expanded form.
solved.solution: 1234 = 1000 + 200 + 30 + 4, that is 1 thousand + 2 hundreds + 3 tens + 4 ones.

solved.problem: A child writes 321 = 3 + 2 + 1. Correct it and name the error.
solved.solution: The child expanded by face value, ignoring place value. Correct form: 321 = 300 + 20 + 1.

hints: Six hundreds, zero tens, five ones.
Two thousands, zero hundreds, five tens, zero ones.

topics.name: Comparison of Numbers
topics.details: Comparing two numbers means deciding which is greater, smaller or whether they are equal, written with the signs >, < and =. The method is short and CTET expects it cleanly applied. First count the digits: a number with more digits is always larger, so 1000 (four digits) beats 999 (three digits) outright. When the digit counts match, compare from the leftmost (highest) place and move right until the first column where the digits differ; the number with the bigger digit there is greater. Comparing 550 and 505, the hundreds match (5 = 5), so move to the tens - 5 against 0 - and since 5 > 0, 550 > 505. The well-known childhood error is to declare 999 bigger than 1000 'because 9 is bigger than 1', focusing on a single eye-catching digit instead of the number of digits and place value. The teacher's job is to steer pupils to count digits first, then compare left to right - never to judge by the largest-looking single digit.

solved.problem: Compare 999 and 1000 using the correct sign.
solved.solution: 1000 > 999. A four-digit number is always greater than a three-digit number, so the count of digits settles it before any digit-by-digit comparison.

solved.problem: Compare 550 and 505.
solved.solution: 550 > 505. Same number of digits; hundreds match (5 = 5), tens differ (5 > 0), so 550 is greater.

solved.problem: A child says 89 is greater than 123 'because 8 is bigger than 1'. Correct this.
solved.solution: 123 > 89. 123 has three digits and 89 has two, so 123 is larger. The child compared leading digits instead of counting digits first.

solved.problem: Compare 4621 and 4628.
solved.solution: 4628 > 4621. Thousands, hundreds and tens all match; the first difference is in the ones place, where 8 > 1.

unsolved.problem: Put the correct sign between 72 and 720.

hints: No need to compare digit by digit.

topics.name: Ordering Numbers
topics.details: Ordering extends comparison to a whole set. Ascending order runs smallest to largest; descending order runs largest to smallest. The procedure is the comparison rule applied repeatedly: group by number of digits first (fewer digits means smaller), then within each group compare from the leftmost place rightwards until a difference shows. Take 321, 45, 3210, 456 in ascending order. The two-digit 45 is smallest; among the three-digit numbers 321 < 456 because 3 < 4 at the hundreds place; the four-digit 3210 is largest - giving 45 < 321 < 456 < 3210. Descending is the same logic reversed: for 505, 55, 550, 5005 the four-digit 5005 leads, the two-digit 55 trails, and between 505 and 550 the tens place decides (0 < 5) so 550 > 505, giving 5005 > 550 > 505 > 55. The misconception to watch is ordering by the leading digit alone - placing 35, 123, 87 as 35, 87, 123 by reading only 3, 8, 1 - when 123 is in fact the largest because it has the most digits.

solved.problem: Arrange in ascending order: 321, 45, 3210, 456.
solved.solution: Group by digits: 45 (2 digits) smallest, then 321 and 456 (3 digits) with 321 < 456, then 3210 (4 digits) largest. Result: 45, 321, 456, 3210.

solved.problem: Arrange in descending order: 505, 55, 550, 5005.
solved.solution: 5005 (4 digits) is largest; 55 (2 digits) smallest; among 505 and 550 the tens place gives 550 > 505. Result: 5005, 550, 505, 55.

solved.problem: A child orders 35, 123, 87 as 35, 87, 123 by reading first digits 3, 8, 1. What is wrong?
solved.solution: The child ignored digit count. 123 has three digits so it is largest; the correct ascending order is 35, 87, 123.

solved.problem: In the ascending arrangement 45, 321, 456, 3210, which number is in the middle two positions if there were a single middle - identify the second-smallest.
solved.solution: The second-smallest is 321 (it follows 45 and precedes 456 and 3210).

hints: One digit, then two, then three.

unsolved.problem: Which number is the largest in the set 78, 708, 87, 780?

topics.name: Number Patterns
topics.details: A number pattern is a sequence built by a fixed rule, and each entry is a term. Spotting the rule lets you extend the sequence or fill a gap, which is the early root of algebraic thinking. The common families: arithmetic patterns add a constant (5, 10, 15, 20 adds 5); geometric patterns multiply by a constant (2, 4, 8, 16 doubles); square numbers come from squaring positions (1, 4, 9, 16, 25 = 1^2, 2^2, 3^2, 4^2, 5^2); triangular numbers add the next counting number each time (1, 3, 6, 10, 15); a Fibonacci-like rule adds the two previous terms (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8); and alternating patterns apply two operations in turn. Consecutive numbers sit next to each other with a fixed gap: consecutive natural numbers differ by 1, consecutive even or odd numbers differ by 2, consecutive multiples of k differ by k. Worth remembering: the sum of two consecutive natural numbers is always odd, and the sum of three consecutive natural numbers is always divisible by 3 (since (n-1) + n + (n+1) = 3n). To find a missing term, test for a common difference, then a multiply rule, then position-based or alternating patterns. The classic error is to fix on the first one or two gaps before checking the whole sequence.

solved.problem: Find the missing number: 7, __, 13, 16, 19.
solved.solution: From 13 to 16 is +3 and 16 to 19 is +3, so the common difference is 3. The missing term is 7 + 3 = 10.

solved.problem: Find the missing number: 3, 6, __, 24, 48.
solved.solution: Each term doubles: 3 x 2 = 6 and 24 x 2 = 48. So the missing term is 6 x 2 = 12.

solved.problem: What are the next two terms: 1, 4, 9, 16, __, __ ?
solved.solution: These are square numbers 1^2, 2^2, 3^2, 4^2, so the next are 5^2 = 25 and 6^2 = 36.

solved.problem: Find the missing number in the alternating sequence: 2, 5, 4, 10, 6, __, 8.
solved.solution: Odd positions 2, 4, 6, 8 increase by 2; even positions 5, 10, __ increase by 5. The missing even-position term is 10 + 5 = 15.

topics.name: Odd and Even Numbers
topics.details: Parity is whether a number is even or odd, and it is decided by one digit only - the units digit. A number is even if it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8; even numbers are exactly divisible by 2 and can be written as 2n, so they pair off with nothing left over. A number is odd if it ends in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9; divided by 2 an odd number leaves remainder 1 and can be written as 2n + 1, so one item is always unpaired. Note that zero is even (0 divided by 2 is 0, no remainder), and only the units digit counts - 3214 is even because it ends in 4, never mind the 3 at the front. The operation rules are heavily tested. Addition and subtraction: even and even give even, odd and odd give even, mixing odd and even gives odd. Multiplication: if any factor is even the product is even, and a product is odd only when every factor is odd (3 x 5 = 15, odd; 6 x 3 = 18, even). Two handy results: the sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2 (1 + 3 = 4 = 2^2; 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4^2), and the sum of the first n even numbers is n(n + 1). The two errors children make most are assuming odd + odd stays odd and judging parity from the first digit rather than the last.

solved.problem: Is 3214 odd or even? How do you know?
solved.solution: Even. Parity is decided by the units digit only, and 3214 ends in 4, which is even. The leading digits are irrelevant.

solved.problem: A child claims odd + odd = odd. Use 3 + 5 to correct this.
solved.solution: 3 + 5 = 8, which is even. Algebraically (2m + 1) + (2n + 1) = 2(m + n + 1), always even. Odd + odd = even.

solved.problem: Without multiplying fully, state whether 6 x 7 is odd or even, and why.
solved.solution: Even. One factor (6) is even, and any product with an even factor is a multiple of 2. (6 x 7 = 42, even.)

solved.problem: Find the sum of the first four odd numbers and state the shortcut.
solved.solution: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4^2. The sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2, so for n = 4 it is 16.

unsolved.problem: Is the product 5 x 9 odd or even?
hints: Odd only when every factor is odd.

topics.name: Roman Numerals (Basic)
topics.details: Roman numerals are the symbol system of ancient Rome, still seen on clocks, chapter headings and monuments. At the primary level five symbols matter: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100. Numbers are built by three rules. The addition rule: a smaller symbol written after (to the right of) a larger one is added, so VI = 5 + 1 = 6 and LXV = 50 + 10 + 5 = 65. The subtraction rule: a smaller symbol written before (to the left of) a larger one is subtracted, so IV = 5 - 1 = 4, IX = 9, XL = 40 and XC = 90 - but only I, X and C are ever subtracted (I from V and X; X from L and C), and V and L are never subtracted. The repetition rule: I, X and C may repeat up to three times to add up (III = 3, XXX = 30), while V and L are never repeated; this is why 4 is IV and never IIII. Symbols normally run largest to smallest, left to right. So XIV reads as X (10) + IV (4) = 14, and XCIX reads as XC (90) + IX (9) = 99.

solved.problem: Convert XIV to a Hindu-Arabic number.
solved.solution: XIV = X + IV = 10 + 4 = 14. The IV uses the subtraction rule (1 before 5 = 4).

solved.problem: Why is 4 written as IV and not IIII?
solved.solution: A symbol may repeat at most three times, so IIII is invalid. The subtraction rule gives IV = 5 - 1 = 4 instead.

solved.problem: Convert XCIX to a number.
solved.solution: XCIX = XC + IX = 90 + 9 = 99. XC is 100 - 10 = 90 and IX is 10 - 1 = 9.

solved.problem: Write 65 in Roman numerals.
solved.solution: LXV = 50 + 10 + 5 = 65, using the addition rule with symbols in largest-to-smallest order.

hints: L is 50, XX is 20, V is 5, III is 3.

shortcuts: Place value of a digit = the digit x the value of its column. In 347 the 4 means 4 x 10 = 40. Face value is just the digit (4).
Comparing numbers: count the digits first - more digits always wins. Only if digit counts match do you compare left to right.
Parity is decided by the LAST digit alone: ends in 0/2/4/6/8 = even, ends in 1/3/5/7/9 = odd. Front digits are irrelevant.
Operation parity: same kind adds to even (even+even, odd+odd both even); mixing gives odd. A product is odd only if every factor is odd.
Roman subtraction cases to memorise: IV=4, IX=9, XL=40, XC=90. Smaller before larger subtracts; smaller after larger adds.
Sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2 (1+3+5+7 = 16 = 4^2) - a quick check for odd-series questions.
mistakes: Confusing face value with place value - in 3582 the face value of 8 is 8 but its place value is 80.
Dropping the placeholder zero - writing "five hundred six" as 56 instead of 506, or expanding 605 without the empty tens column.
Comparing or ordering by the leading digit instead of counting digits first - calling 89 bigger than 123 because 8 beats 1.
Believing odd + odd = odd; it is even, because the two unpaired units join to form a new pair.
Judging parity from the first digit - 3214 is even because it ends in 4, not odd because it starts with 3.
Writing 4 as IIII in Roman numerals - a symbol repeats at most three times, so 4 is IV.
pyq: Numbers appears in every CTET Paper I, typically 6-9 marks split between the Mathematics content questions and the Maths-Pedagogy questions. Content items are direct: state the place value of a digit, write a number in expanded form, convert a Roman numeral (XIV, XL, XCIX are favourites), continue a pattern, or decide parity. The pedagogy items are scenario-driven and higher-value - a child writes 506 as 56 (zero as placeholder), orders 35, 123, 87 wrongly by leading digit (must group by digit count), or insists odd + odd is odd - and you must name the misconception and the concrete remedy (base-10 blocks, pairing counters, number-line skip counting). Examiners reliably reward candidates who can explain the underlying place value or parity idea rather than just produce the right answer.

summary: Numbers and the number system underpins all of CTET Paper I maths. Counting rests on stable order, one-to-one correspondence and cardinality, and grows through forward, backward and skip counting. Place value - the value of a digit from its column (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands) - drives number names, expanded form, comparison and ordering, with the face-value-versus-place-value distinction and zero-as-placeholder being the most tested traps. Comparing and ordering both start by counting digits, then compare left to right. Patterns build algebraic thinking through arithmetic, geometric, square, triangular and consecutive-number rules. Parity is fixed by the units digit (even ends 0/2/4/6/8, odd ends 1/3/5/7/9), with even+even and odd+odd both even and a product odd only when all factors are odd. Roman numerals use I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100 with add, subtract (IV, IX, XL, XC) and repetition rules. Throughout, the exam pairs the arithmetic with the classroom - naming children's misconceptions and the concrete remedies that fix them.
